# Data protection along the entire data flow {#sec-b23}

<!-- page-provenance:start -->
::: {.page-provenance}
*R. Heller · Date: 2025-10-19 · Last changed: 2026-11-09*
:::
<!-- page-provenance:end -->



::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## At a glance

**Guiding question:** Who receives which data, for what purpose, and for how long?\
**For:** clinical researchers, data stewards, teachers who want to show real examples, and reviewers; the core reading
needs no programming. · **Prerequisites:** the gait measurement from video in @sec-b11; how data arise in @sec-b03;
the regulatory note in @sec-b22 helps but is not required.\
**In the course:** [W7 · Regulation, data protection and
incident](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w7-regulation-data-protection-incident.html)
(data flow and DPIA screening); also used in W1, W2, W4 and
[W8](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w8-colloquium-and-decision.html) ·
**Data:** synthetic (data-flow register generated in the chapter); legal status checked on 8 November 2026 ·
**Core reading time:** about 11 minutes
:::

## Case and decision {#sec-b23-case}

The rehabilitation clinic of @sec-b11 films patients walking after surgery for a tibial plateau fracture. The videos
support treatment decisions. A research team wants to compare video-based knee angles with the marker-based reference
method, and a lecturer wants one clip for a seminar. An external service provider offers cloud pose estimation that
turns video into body keypoints (hip, knee, ankle and other landmarks) within minutes. By Friday the study lead has to
decide what leaves the clinic: the raw videos, the keypoints, or only the angles. She must also say who holds the
list linking study numbers to patients, and when each copy is deleted. She decides that keypoints are extracted on
site, that the provider receives no video, and that the seminar uses a synthetic clip. The study starts three weeks
later than planned, but no copy exists whose purpose and deletion date are unknown.

## Core reading {#sec-b23-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · required for W7 · about 11 minutes · ends before ‘Decision exercise’
:::

**Follow the copies, not the project.** Data protection questions become answerable when every copy of the data is
drawn as a step with a purpose, a holder and an end. @fig-b23-flow traces a gait video from the camera to a knee angle
in a research table. It marks where people are directly identifiable, where data are pseudonymised, where the
boundary of the controlling institution is crossed and where each copy is deleted. All statements on law refer to the
[GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj/eng) and German law as of
8 November 2026 [@eu2016dsgvo].


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}

Boxes are copies or processing steps; the prefix gives the identifiability: D = directly identifying, P = pseudonymised (still personal data), S = synthetic. Shaded areas are organisational boundaries. Crosses mark deletion points; days are assumptions to be set locally. Fictional flow; no data.](b23-data-protection_files/figure-epub/fig-b23-flow-1.png){#fig-b23-flow fig-alt='Diagram with three shaded areas. The largest, the clinic as controller, contains a chain of boxes from left to right: D gait video at capture, D clinic video store, D on-site pose estimation, P keypoint series, P knee angle per stride, and P research table. :::


**Two legal questions, asked separately.** A gait video recorded for treatment shows a person's body, face and
condition. It is personal data and, because it reveals information about health, data concerning health. Each
processing step therefore needs two answers that must not be merged. First, a lawful basis under Art. 6(1) GDPR, for
example the performance of a treatment contract or a task in the public interest [Law]. Second, an exception from the
prohibition on processing special categories under Art. 9(2), for example medical diagnosis and treatment under a
duty of professional secrecy (Art. 9(2)(h) with 9(3)) or research based on Union or Member State law with suitable
safeguards (Art. 9(2)(j)) [Law]. A step with an Art. 6 basis but no Art. 9 exception is unlawful, and the reverse as
well. As in @sec-b22, the labels [Law], [Guidance], [Interpretation] and [Local] mark the kind of statement.

**Care, research and teaching are different purposes.** @tbl-b23-purposes compares them. Research has its own
routes: consent (Art. 6(1)(a) with 9(2)(a)) or a statutory research provision under Art. 9(2)(j). In Germany, the
Federal Data Protection Act (Bundesdatenschutzgesetz, BDSG),
[§ 27](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/bdsg_2018/__27.html), permits processing special categories for research
without consent if it is necessary and the controller's interest substantially outweighs the person's interest in
exclusion, with specific safeguards [@bdsg27; Law]. The BDSG applies to federal public bodies and to private bodies;
to public bodies of the federal states it applies only in narrow cases where state law does not regulate data
protection (§ 1(1)) [Law]. Whether a hospital falls under § 27 BDSG, a state hospital or data protection act, or
the Health Data Use Act (Gesundheitsdatennutzungsgesetz, GDNG),
[§ 6](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/gdng/__6.html), which lets health institutions further process their own care data for
research if the data are pseudonymised and personal data are generally not passed to third parties [@gdng6; Law], is a
[Local] question for the data protection officer. **The key assumption: calling an activity "research" exempts
nothing by itself; a specific legal provision with its conditions has to fit the specific step.** Teaching is not
research, so no research provision covers the seminar clip [Interpretation].

| | Care | Research | Teaching |
|---|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Treatment decision for this patient | Agreement of two angle measurements | Showing students what a gait pattern looks like |
| Art. 6 GDPR | Treatment contract or legal obligation (Art. 6(1)(b), (c)) | Consent or public task (Art. 6(1)(a), (e)) | Consent (Art. 6(1)(a)) |
| Art. 9 GDPR | Art. 9(2)(h) with professional secrecy (9(3)) | Art. 9(2)(a) consent, or 9(2)(j) with national law | Art. 9(2)(a) explicit consent |
| National law | Professional and hospital law [Local] | § 27 BDSG, state law or § 6 GDNG – whichever applies [Local] | None that replaces consent [Interpretation] |
| Who sees raw video | Treating team | Nobody outside the on-site extraction step | Nobody: synthetic clip |
| Deletion | End of care retention period [Local] | Research video copy after keypoint QC; key table at end of retention period | Not applicable for synthetic data |

: Care, research and teaching use of the same gait video. Fictional case; legal status 8 November 2026; bracketed labels mark interpretation and local questions. {#tbl-b23-purposes}

**Pseudonymisation is not anonymisation.** The GDPR defines pseudonymisation as processing such that data can no
longer be attributed to a specific person without additional information that is kept separately and protected
(Art. 4(5)) [Law]. The additional information here is the key table. It needs a named holder (for example a data
custodian outside the research team), a written rule for when re-identification is allowed (withdrawal of consent, an
incidental finding) and a deletion date. Pseudonymised data remain personal data for the controller. The Court of
Justice held in 2025 that pseudonymised data need not be personal data "in all cases and for every person": for a
recipient who cannot lift the pseudonymisation and cannot identify the person by other means, including by
cross-checking with other factors, they may not be; but the controller's duty to inform people about recipients is
assessed at collection, from the controller's point of view [@cjeu2025srb, paras 77, 86, 111–112]. The judgment
concerned the parallel regulation for EU institutions; its transfer to the GDPR is plausible but remains
[Interpretation]. For gait it matters a great deal: movement itself can identify. In one study, 95% of 511 people were
recognised from less than five minutes of virtual-reality motion tracking data [@miller2020motion; *published*]. Keypoint
series should therefore be treated as personal data at every recipient unless the opposite has been shown.

**Roles and borders.** The clinic, as the body that decides on purposes and means, is the controller (Art. 4(7))
[Law]. A cloud service that estimates poses on its instructions is a processor; this requires a contract that, among
other things, binds it to documented instructions and to deletion or return of data at the end (Art. 28(3)) [Law]. If
the provider stores data or provides support from outside the European Economic Area, the transfer rules of Chapter V
apply: an adequacy decision (Art. 45) or appropriate safeguards such as standard contractual clauses (Art. 46)
[Law]. People keep their rights to information, access, rectification, erasure and objection (Art. 13–21); for
research, restrictions exist only where Union or Member State law provides them (Art. 89(2); § 27(2) BDSG) [Law].

**When is a DPIA needed?** A data protection impact assessment is required where processing is likely to result in a
high risk, in particular for large-scale processing of special categories (Art. 35(1), 35(3)(b)) [Law]. "Large scale"
has no number in the text; the supervisory authorities publish lists of processing that requires a DPIA
(Art. 35(4)) [Law; Local]. New technology, health data and a cloud provider make a documented screening the minimum
[Interpretation].

**Question for the workshop:** Your clinic wants to keep the raw research copy of each video "in case a better pose
model appears". Which purpose, legal basis and deletion date would you have to write down to allow this, and would you
sign it?

## Decision exercise {#sec-b23-exercise}

**Role task.** Work in four roles: study lead, data protection officer, clinic IT and a patient representative. Trace
the data flow of @fig-b23-flow step by step. For each step write down: data, identifiability, purpose, Art. 6 basis,
Art. 9 exception, role of the holder, location, transfer mechanism (if outside the EEA), deletion point and residual
re-identification risk. The patient representative may veto any step whose purpose cannot be explained in one sentence.

**A register that checks itself.** The register can be written as a small table in R with explicit rules. This does
not replace a legal assessment; it makes omissions visible.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Data-flow register for the fictional gait study (one row per copy or processing step)
register <- data.frame(
  step      = c("capture", "clinic_store", "pose_onsite", "keypoints", "angles", "research_table",
                "key_table", "teaching_clip"),
  level     = c("direct", "direct", "direct", "pseudonymised", "pseudonymised", "pseudonymised",
                "direct", "synthetic"),
  purpose   = c("care", "care", "research", "research", "research", "research", "research", "teaching"),
  art6      = c("6(1)(b)", "6(1)(c)", "6(1)(a)", "6(1)(a)", "6(1)(a)", "6(1)(a)", "6(1)(a)", NA),
  art9      = c("9(2)(h)", "9(2)(h)", "9(2)(a)", "9(2)(a)", "9(2)(a)", "9(2)(a)", "9(2)(a)", NA),
  holder    = c("clinic", "clinic", "clinic", "clinic", "clinic", "clinic", "data custodian", "lecturer"),
  processor = c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE),
  art28     = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA),
  location  = c("EU", "EU", "EU", "EU", "EU", "EU", "EU", "EU"),
  chapter_v = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA),
  deletion  = c("after transfer to store", "care retention period (local)", "after keypoint QC, day 30",
                "end of study", "end of study", "retention period (local)", "retention period (local)", NA),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Rules: each returns the steps that violate it
check_register <- function(r) {
  personal <- r$level != "synthetic"
  list(
    missing_art6        = r$step[personal & is.na(r$art6)],
    missing_art9        = r$step[personal & (is.na(r$art9) | r$art9 == "none")],
    processor_no_art28  = r$step[r$processor & (is.na(r$art28) | r$art28 != "contract")],
    third_country_no_v  = r$step[r$location != "EU" & is.na(r$chapter_v)],
    personal_no_delete  = r$step[personal & is.na(r$deletion)],
    teaching_real_data  = r$step[r$purpose == "teaching" & personal & r$art9 != "9(2)(a)"]
  )
}
result <- check_register(register)
result
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> $missing_art6
#> character(0)
#> 
#> $missing_art9
#> character(0)
#> 
#> $processor_no_art28
#> character(0)
#> 
#> $third_country_no_v
#> character(0)
#> 
#> $personal_no_delete
#> character(0)
#> 
#> $teaching_real_data
#> character(0)
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Expected result: no rule is violated
stopifnot(all(lengths(result) == 0))
```
:::


**Expected result.** A register in which every personal-data step has both an Art. 6 basis and an Art. 9 exception,
every copy has a deletion point, the key table has a named holder and the seminar uses synthetic data. Learners also
write one sentence on the residual risk: "Keypoint series and angles remain re-identifiable through movement patterns
and visit dates; they are shared only within the clinic."\
**Alternative.** The cloud provider is used under an Art. 28 contract with EU-only processing and deletion after
return of results. This is lawful in principle but adds a recipient, a contract to monitor and a possible transfer
question if support staff work from outside the EEA.\
**Residual question.** Who checks, a year from now, that the research copy of each video really was deleted on day 30?

**The incident clock.** In the fictional incident of @sec-b24, the service provider tells the hospital on a Monday
morning that a radiology report excerpt appeared in its support log. A processor must inform the controller without
undue delay (Art. 33(2)); the controller notifies the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming
aware, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to people's rights and freedoms (Art. 33(1)) [Law]. The
EDPB considers a controller "aware" when it has a reasonable degree of certainty that a security incident has led to
personal data being compromised [@edpb2023breach, para. 31; Guidance].


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Fictional times (Europe/Berlin); awareness = reasonable certainty after the first check
provider_message <- as.POSIXct("2026-11-09 07:40", tz = "Europe/Berlin")
aware            <- as.POSIXct("2026-11-09 10:30", tz = "Europe/Berlin")
deadline_33      <- aware + 72 * 3600
# English day and month names regardless of the computer's locale
fmt_time <- function(x) {
  sprintf("%s %s %s %s, %s", c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")[as.integer(format(x, "%u"))],
          format(x, "%d"), month.abb[as.integer(format(x, "%m"))], format(x, "%Y"), format(x, "%H:%M"))
}
data.frame(event = c("processor informs controller", "controller aware", "72 hours end"),
           time = fmt_time(c(provider_message, aware, deadline_33)))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                          event                   time
#> 1 processor informs controller Mon 09 Nov 2026, 07:40
#> 2             controller aware Mon 09 Nov 2026, 10:30
#> 3                 72 hours end Thu 12 Nov 2026, 10:30
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# The 72 hours run from awareness, not from the end of the analysis: Thursday, 10:30
stopifnot(format(deadline_33, "%u") == "4", deadline_33 - aware == as.difftime(72, units = "hours"))
```
:::


The clock is only one part of the decision. Three further questions must be answered by named people, not by code:
is a risk to the people affected unlikely (then no notification, but documentation under Art. 33(5)); is the risk
likely to be high (then the people must also be informed under Art. 34(1), unless one of the conditions of Art. 34(3)
applies, for example data rendered unintelligible by encryption); and if notification comes after 72 hours, what are
the reasons for the delay? [Law]

## Counter-check {#sec-b23-countercheck}

Change one assumption and predict which rule fails before you run the code. Version 1: the clinic chooses the cloud
provider, whose support team works from a third country, and the contract has not yet been signed. Version 2: the
lecturer replaces the synthetic clip with a real patient video "because it is more convincing", without consent.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Version 1: cloud pose estimation instead of on-site extraction
v1 <- register
v1$holder[3]    <- "cloud provider"
v1$processor[3] <- TRUE
v1$location[3]  <- "third country"
# Version 2: real video in the seminar without consent
v2 <- register
v2$level[8] <- "direct"; v2$art6[8] <- "6(1)(e)"; v2$art9[8] <- "none"; v2$deletion[8] <- "end of term"
failed <- function(r) names(Filter(length, check_register(r)))
list(version_1 = failed(v1), version_2 = failed(v2))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> $version_1
#> [1] "processor_no_art28" "third_country_no_v"
#> 
#> $version_2
#> [1] "missing_art9"       "teaching_real_data"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(identical(failed(v1), c("processor_no_art28", "third_country_no_v")),
          identical(failed(v2), c("missing_art9", "teaching_real_data")))
```
:::


Version 1 fails twice: there is no processor contract and no Chapter V mechanism. Both can be repaired, but only
before the first video leaves the clinic. Version 2 fails twice: the step has no Art. 9 exception, and a real patient video in teaching needs explicit
consent; no research provision covers a seminar. A public-task basis for teaching (Art. 6(1)(e)) would still lack an
Art. 9 exception [Interpretation]. If the rule set had only one column "legal basis", version 2 would have passed.
This is the practical reason for keeping Art. 6 and Art. 9 apart.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b23-consequences}

**An open question changes the plan.** Whether keypoint series are personal data for the cloud provider cannot be
settled without knowing what else the provider holds. The judgment of 2025 makes the answer depend on the recipient's
actual means of identification [@cjeu2025srb], and the motion study suggests that those means may be small
[@miller2020motion]. The study team therefore plans as if they were personal data. @tbl-b23-plan shows the effect.

| Element | Plan before the review | Plan after the review |
|---|---|---|
| Pose estimation | Cloud service, video upload | On-site extraction; provider receives no video |
| Raw research copy | Kept "for later models" | Deleted after keypoint quality control (day 30, assumption) |
| Key table | In the study folder | Held by a data custodian; re-identification only for withdrawal or incidental findings |
| Seminar | Real patient clip | Synthetic gait clip; real clips only with explicit consent and a deletion date |
| DPIA | "Not needed for a small study" | Documented screening; full DPIA if the supervisory authority's list or the data volume requires it |
| Information sheet | Generic | Names recipients, purposes, retention and the contact for withdrawal |

: Deployment plan for the gait study before and after the data-protection review. Fictional plan. {#tbl-b23-plan}

**For patients**, the change means that their face and walk do not leave the clinic and that they can find out who
holds a copy. **Ethics** (@sec-b21): patients with rare injuries or visible impairments are easier to recognise; a
small group needs more protection, not less. **Regulation** (@sec-b22): if the angle is used for treatment decisions,
the software may become a medical device. **Security** (@sec-b24): the key table and the video store are the assets
whose confidentiality matters most.

::: {.callout-note title="The incident from the data-protection perspective"}
Which personal data were accessible to whom, who assesses the risk, and who decides on notification and
communication? The controller decides, advised by the data protection officer; the processor only reports. The
assessment starts from facts: which report excerpts, how many people, who could read the support log, and whether the
log has been deleted at the provider. A notification under Art. 33 is required unless a risk is unlikely; it should be
made, where feasible, within 72 hours of awareness, and may be completed in phases (Art. 33(4)). Informing the people
affected is a separate decision with a higher threshold – a likely high risk – and its own exceptions (Art. 34) [Law].
The technical restart (@sec-b24) has a different trigger, a different owner and a different end point; a good
handover names both.
:::

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b23-lookup}

**Reviewer question.** Does the manuscript state which data left the institution, in which form, to whom and on which
legal basis, and how long copies were kept? "Data were pseudonymised" without saying who held the key, and whether
recipients could re-identify, is not a description of a safeguard.

**Self-test.** The supplier of the fracture alert in @sec-b09 asks the emergency department to send "the original
DICOM images" of 30 false alarms so that it can check the model. What do you send, and what must be in place first?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
First ask what the check needs. To review a false alarm the supplier needs the pixel data, the region the tool marked
and perhaps acquisition parameters – not names, dates of birth or accession numbers, which DICOM headers usually
contain. Data minimisation (Art. 5(1)(c)) and data protection by design (Art. 25) point to images with identifying
header fields removed, or to a review session inside the hospital's systems [Law; Interpretation]. Burned-in text in
the image must be checked as well. Before anything is sent, the roles must be clear: if the supplier processes the
images on the hospital's behalf, an Art. 28 contract with deletion after the check is needed; if it wants to use them
to improve its product, it decides on its own purposes and needs its own legal basis [Interpretation; Local]. If the
supplier works from outside the EEA, Chapter V applies. The images remain health data even without names, because the
hospital can re-identify them.
:::

**Annotated sources.**

- @eu2016dsgvo – the GDPR, from Art. 4 definitions to Art. 33–35; the binding text for every step in the register.
- @bdsg27 and @gdng6 – two German research provisions with different addressees and conditions; neither applies
  automatically.
- @cjeu2025srb – the 2025 judgment on pseudonymised data at the recipient and on the controller's duty to inform.
- @miller2020motion – published evidence that movement data identify people.
- @edpb2023breach – EDPB guidance on breach notification, including when a controller becomes "aware".
- @edpb2025pseudonymisation – EDPB guidance on pseudonymisation and the "pseudonymisation domain" (version for public
  consultation).

## Further reading {#sec-b23-further}

- @sec-b11 – how the knee angle is computed from keypoints and why raw video may still be needed for quality control.
- @sec-b03 – how small, rare groups in a table make people recognisable.
- @sec-b24 – protecting the key table, the video store and the logs.
- @sec-b26 – secondary use, controlled access and the stepwise application of the European Health Data Space
  Regulation, whose chapter on secondary use applies from 26 March 2029 (Art. 105) [@eu2025ehds].
- [Methods in R: The research workflow](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-appendices-a-research-workflow.html#sec-appendices-a-research-workflow-4-acquisition)
  – where data acquisition and its documentation sit in a project.
- [Scientometrics in R: Reproducible pipelines](https://cttir.github.io/scientometrics-in-r/reproducible-pipelines.html)
  – documenting each processing step so that a register can be kept up to date.
- [CTTIR Courses: Research workflow](https://cttir.github.io/courses/appendices/research_workflow.html) – planning
  data handling before the first measurement.
- [CTTIR Courses: Import, joins, and missingness with dplyr](https://cttir.github.io/courses/course1_foundations/labs/lab_week1_session4.html)
  – the joins that a key table makes possible, and therefore why it must be guarded.
